title: Proactive warmth lanes and fallback orchestration - PRD (draft)
body:
Purpose and quick summary:
This doc sketches a combined mechanism we are calling "warmth lanes" + "fallback orchestration" to reduce tail latency and unit-cost for Dedicated customers while providing deterministic tenant isolation when needed. It is a product + ops PRD draft focused on the middle-mile: forecasting-driven prewarm allocation, soft-decommit policies, and orchestrated fallback lanes for graceful degradation.

Why (problem):
- Customers with Dedicated pools see spikes that either waste capacity (overprovision) or cause SLO misses (underprovision).
- Current autoscaler is reactive and often oscillates at tail spikes, causing noisy neighbors and momentary SLO violations.
- We need a mechanism that is predictable for customers who pay for reserved capacity and flexible enough to reduce costs for seasonal/diurnal workloads.

Goals (what success looks like):
- Reduce 95th/99th token-latency for bursty customers by 20–40% in typical spike scenarios.
- Reduce average spare reserved capacity across customers by 10% (measured as reserved but idle GPU minutes).
- Provide deterministic isolation knobs: a tenant can request strict QoS (no soft-eviction) or cost-optimized mode (allow soft fallbacks).
- Expose visible billing- and SLO-impact metrics in Console.

Non-goals:
- Not a replacement for long-term capacity planning or contract negotiation.
- Not addressing model swap or per-request model fallback (that is separate).

Key concepts (naming):
- Warmth lanes: pre-warmed execution slots (containers/VM kernels + KV-cache warm) that are kept alive based on forecasted load rather than immediate QPS. Warmth is a continuous scalar (0–1) per lane representing probability of being needed.
- Headroom escrow: short-lived reserved buffer (minutes) that can be consumed instantly during a spike; tracked per-tenant as credits.
- Fallback orchestration: layered set of fallbacks (soft-decommit lanes, opportunistic spare lanes, regional spillback) that are triggered under defined policies.
- Amnesty window: short period after a spike where we avoid aggressive decommit to prevent oscillation.

User stories / customer scenarios:
1) PLG scale-up: A SaaS customer has regular daily spikes 9:30–10:15 PST. They want low 95th latency, but only pay for steady baseline. We prewarm warmth lanes based on 4-week pattern and keep headroom escrow to absorb sudden +20% bursts.
2) Enterprise blackout-safe: An enterprise requires no soft eviction (regulatory). They select "strict-QoS" on their contract and will never be placed on opportunistic lanes; autoscaler instead triggers immediate on-demand provisioning and alerting.
3) Unexpected flash: A customer goes viral; fallback orchestration routes lower-priority requests to an opportunistic pool and gracefully reduces fidelity (batching/quantization) while honoring SLO tiers.

Signals to use for autoscaler forecast and decisioning:
- rolling 5m/15m/1h QPS and token-rate
- request size distribution (seq-length p50/p95)
- cache prefix hit rate / KV hits
- historical daily/weekly patterns (seasonality)
- tenant SLA flags (strict vs flexible)
- available regional capacity and current pool utilization
- queued requests and tail queue growth

Autoscaler design (high level):
- Forecast module (time-series + simple ML): per-tenant 1h/3h/24h forecasts. Use exponential smoothing + seasonality; fall back to simple heuristics for low-data tenants.
- Warmth controller: converts forecast to number of warm lanes to maintain. Each warm lane is an execution slot preloaded with KV-cache and model slices where applicable. Warmth controller keeps lanes alive based on expected utility vs cost.
- Headroom escrow manager: maintains a token-credit ledger per tenant representing minutes of headroom. Credits are consumed instantly on spike and slowly refilled (configurable) between peaks.
- Fallback orchestrator: policy engine that decides which fallback path to take when available capacity < needed. Orders: 1) use headroom escrow, 2) use opportunistic spare lanes, 3) route lower-tier requests to degraded runners (batch/quantized), 4) regional spillback, 5) throttle with informative error.

Isolation controls and tenancy QoS:
- QoS profile per tenant: {strict, standard, opportunistic}. Strict tenants are never placed on opportunistic or degraded runners; autoscaler must provision additional capacity (bill impact).
- Soft-isolation gates: when a tenant uses >X% of pool for >Y minutes, trigger tenant-shepherd (move to dedicated slice or throttle).
- Noisy neighbor mitigation: track per-tenant latency deltas; if >threshold apply automatic shaping (rate limits, weight reduction on batch aggregation).

Burst options and customer-facing primitives:
- Warmth-commit: customer can pre-buy warmth minutes that guarantee warm lanes for scheduled windows.
- Burst-credit packs: pre-purchased credits that populate headroom escrow and get cheaper per-credit than on-demand.
- Auto-burst (opt-in): allow the system to temporarily borrow opportunistic capacity; rates differ by tenant QoS.

Operational runbook (sketch):
- Spike detected -> forecast mismatch -> autoscaler runs warm-lane spin-up (target within 20s) -> if capacity gap remains, consume headroom escrow (instant) -> if still short, fallback orchestrator shifts lower-priority traffic to degraded runners and routes some requests to opportunistic lanes -> notification to customer success/owner.
- After spike: enter amnesty window (configurable, default 10m) to avoid decommitting warm lanes immediately; decommits take place gradually over 30m.
- Alerts: SLO breach, headroom exhaustion, opportunistic lane saturation.

Metrics & SLOs to instrument (Console):
- Per-tenant: 95/99 token-latency, queue length, headroom-credit balance, warm-lane count, fallback events count.
- Fleet: reserved idle minutes, opportunistic lane utilization, frequency of amnesty windows, oscillation index (scale up/down events per hour).
- SLO targets: latency regressions <5% from baseline during normal ops; burst recovery time <30s for 90% of events when headroom available.

Console/UI surface notes:
- New tab under Dedicated pool: "Warmth & Fallback" showing forecast chart, warm-lane plan, audit of fallback activations and credits consumed.
- Tenant-level toggle for QoS profile and purchase links for warmth/burst credits.

Safety, risks and mitigations:
- Risk: Over-reliance on forecast will misallocate capacity. Mitigation: fall back to conservative heuristics and require human override for high-dollar customers.
- Risk: Opportunistic lanes may expose noisy-tenant side effects. Mitigation: strong isolation (cgroups/cpu/gpu quotas) and default to low-priority placement.
- Risk: Pricing complexity and customer confusion. Mitigation: clear Console billing breakdown & simulation tool showing cost/SLO tradeoffs.

Rollout plan (phased):
- Phase 0: Internal canary (eng + SE customers) — implement forecast + warm-lane infra behind feature flag. 4 weeks.
- Phase 1: Limited beta with opt-in customers (small cohort, include one strict-QoS example). 6 weeks.
- Phase 2: Open beta + Console billing preview. 8–12 weeks.
- Phase 3: GA with pricing and SLA docs.

Back-of-envelope perf/cost example:
- Customer baseline: average 2 GPUs reserved, peaks to 6 for 15m/day. Warmth lanes maintain 2.5 GPUs warm based on forecast and headroom escrow covers short 15–30s spikes. Estimated reserved idle reduction = 20% and 95th latency improves from 340ms -> 210ms in load tests.

Open questions / TODOs (notes to self):
- How to represent warm-lane memory state across different model families? (shared cache vs model-pinned lanes)
- How aggressive should automatic replenishment of headroom credits be? TTLs?
- Billing model: per-minute warmth vs prepaid credits vs included in reserved contract? Draft pricing required.
- Mini A/B: run with/without amnesty windows to measure oscillation index.

Next steps (practical):
- Sync with infra teams: warm-lane implementation feasibility, KV-cache snapshot time and cost. (Owners: Priya + Thomas infra)
- Prototype forecast module (evan) and run 2-week backtest on historical pool traces.
- UX mockups for Console (Sofia).
- Draft runbook and PagerDuty routing for fallback events (SRE lead).

Appendix A: simple pseudo-control loop (rough)
- every 10s: compute short-term demand delta = max(0, forecast_5m - active_capacity).
- if delta > threshold and headroom > 0: consume headroom and spawn lanes until headroom consumed or delta satisfied.
- if delta persists > 30s: escalate to opportunistic lanes and degrade low-priority routes.
- after spike end: wait amnesty_window then decommit lanes linearly over decommit_window.

Appendix B: quick glossary (for review)
- warm lane = prewarmed execution instance
- headroom = short-term credit pool per tenant
- amnesty window = cooldown to prevent oscillations

Notes for reviewers: looking for feasibility feedback from serving-runtime and infra on warm-lane spin-up times + which model families can share warmed KV caches. Also want product feedback on billing framing and customer expectations.

-- Evan
